dropped.current: electrified by a private company, providing clean
dropped.proposed: electrified by a private company that provides clean
dropped.printed: His town of Wanyjok was electrified by a private company, providing clean, reliable, and affordable power to his business and his neighbors.
dropped.reason: Misattached participle. A comma-separated -ing phrase at the end of a sentence normally takes the subject of the main clause as its subject. Here that subject is "His town", but a town cannot be "providing power"; the provider is the agent in the by-phrase, "a private company". Students who memorise this sentence would learn a construction that teachers mark wrong (the logical subject of an adverbial participle should be the sentence subject). Changing it to a relative clause attaches the phrase to the company and keeps the meaning. Simply deleting the comma ("a private company providing clean …") also works. Low severity: the meaning is clear, and some editors would accept it as a loose resultative participle ("the electrification provided power").
why: This is not a definite error. The -ing phrase comes right after "a private company", so it reads naturally as a non-restrictive postmodifier of that noun, the way "a company, which provides ..." would. It can also be read as a loose resultative supplement (the electrification provided power). Both are normal in edited journalism, and the meaning is clear. A careful editor would not mark this wrong, and the proposer itself concedes that some editors accept it. Rewriting it as "that provides" is a style change, not a correction. (I could not search the web for the original article because the shared search budget was used up, so this verdict rests on the printed page and grammar alone.)

The current text matches the printed page. After a comma, a sentence-final -ing phrase is taken to refer to the subject ("His town"), and a town cannot provide power. A demanding teacher would mark this misattached participle, so the error is real. A smaller fix than adding "that provides" is to delete the comma. "providing ..." then plainly describes "a private company", no words change or are added, and the tense needs no decision.

"They" also comes right after "their inflated sense", where "their" means the employee, so a reader first takes "They’d" as the employee. why: The text matches the print, but the paragraph refers to the leader as 'he or she' and to the employee as 'they/their' ('their demands', 'their inflated sense', 'their desired rewards'). 'They’d' suddenly switches to 'they' for the leader, right after 'their' meant the employee. That is a pronoun shift with misleading reference, and the modal also shifts from will to would. Teachers and editors mark pronoun shifts as errors. 'He or she will then go further' restores consistency with the previous sentence and keeps the meaning.

Singular 'they' for the leader is standard, and conditional 'would' after 'will' is acceptable in this hypothetical context. 'the employee' later in the same sentence makes the referent clear. Rewriting to 'He or she will' is a stylistic consistency change, not the correction of an error.
